questions.question: Define the mechanical advantage of a gear pair from teeth and from diameters, calculate it for a 15-tooth driver meshed with a 60-tooth driven gear and for a 30 millimetre gear driving a 120 millimetre gear, and explain its relation to velocity ratio and to friction.
questions.expected_answer: The mechanical advantage of a gear pair is the torque at the driven gear over the torque at the driver, which equals driven teeth over driver teeth because teeth pass one for one at the mesh: 60 over 15 gives 4. Since meshing gears share a tooth size, teeth are proportional to pitch diameter, so diameters give the same ratio: 120 over 30 gives 4. The mechanical advantage equals the velocity ratio, the number of driver turns per driven turn, so the driven gear turns four times slower and four times harder. Work in equals work out apart from friction, and friction at the teeth and bearings makes the measured advantage a little below the tooth ratio; the ideal value from teeth is used to design and the measured value, from a spring balance at the drum, is reported in evaluation.

questions.question: Calculate the output speed of a 3 000 revolutions per minute motor through a 15 to 60 pair and through two such stages, explain how compound stages multiply and what idlers and shared shafts contribute, and show how direction and lifting speed follow from the train.
questions.expected_answer: Driven speed is driver speed divided by the velocity ratio: 3 000 over 4 gives 750 revolutions per minute for one stage; two stages give 4 times 4, 16, and 3 000 over 16 gives 187.5 revolutions per minute. In a compound train two gears fixed on one shaft turn together, a large gear driven by the previous stage and a small gear driving the next, so the overall ratio is the product of driven over driver teeth at every mesh; an idler contributes a factor of one and a shared shaft is not a mesh and contributes nothing. Each mesh reverses direction, so a two-stage train turns the output the same way as the motor and a three-stage train the opposite, with an idler flipping it back. Lifting speed is drum revolutions per minute times drum circumference: at 16 to 1 a 40 millimetre drum winds about 23 metres per minute, too fast, while at 64 to 1 it winds about 6 metres per minute, about 10 seconds for a one metre lift.

questions.question: Set out the six-step design calculation for a model winder gear train lifting a 3 newton cage with a motor that can supply 0.2 newtons at the drum, including the margin, the speed check and the effect of drum diameter.
questions.expected_answer: Find the load, about 3 newtons on the rope; measure the effort the bare motor supplies at the drum used, about 0.2 newtons; divide to get the required mechanical advantage, 15, and add a margin for friction and a heavier cage to about 25; choose stages from the kit whose ratios multiply to at least 25, such as two stages of 60 over 12 giving 25, or add a stage if the product falls short; check speed, since 3 000 over 25 gives 120 revolutions per minute, about 15 metres per minute on a 40 millimetre drum, too fast, so raise the ratio towards 60 for about 6 metres per minute or use a smaller drum, which also lowers the torque needed because the rope acts at a smaller radius; check direction by counting meshes and fix it with an idler, the winding sense or motor reversal; and record the train as a list of stages with the overall ratio, direction and lift speed.
